explanations.explanation: Night it is, friend. The songwriter pairs the two: His loving devotion in the morning and His faithfulness at night (Psalm 92:2). So the singing covers sunrise and sundown. I bake early and I bake late, and apparently praise fits on that same schedule.

Harvest is a good guess, but it's not in this line. The songwriter says to proclaim His loving devotion in the morning and His faithfulness at night (Psalm 92:2). Notice it's about times of day, not seasons. Morning and night, with the whole day in between.

Feasts sounds like a party word, and I respect that. But the line says to proclaim His loving devotion in the morning and His faithfulness at night (Psalm 92:2). It's a time of day, not an event. That's the songwriter's pair: morning and night.

Yes, friend. The songwriter says, “For You, O LORD, have made me glad by Your deeds; I sing for joy at the works of Your hands.” (Psalm 92:4) So the gladness comes from what the LORD has done. The song is a thank-you note with a tune.

Laws are a fair guess, since the Bible has plenty of them. But this verse says something different: “For You, O LORD, have made me glad by Your deeds…” (Psalm 92:4). The gladness comes from what the LORD has done. His deeds, friend, His deeds.

Angels would make a fine song, but they're not in this verse. The songwriter says the LORD made him glad “by Your deeds” and that he sings for joy “at the works of Your hands.” (Psalm 92:4) It's all about what the LORD Himself has done. I think that's a pretty good reason to sing.

True, and you can quote it. The songwriter says, “How great are Your works, O LORD, how deep are Your thoughts!” (Psalm 92:5) So the works are great and the thoughts are deep. Two compliments in one breath.

Not false, friend. The verse says, “How great are Your works, O LORD, how deep are Your thoughts!” (Psalm 92:5) So he does say the thoughts are deep. He praises the works and the thoughts together, a double helping.

Destroyed is right. The songwriter says that though the wicked sprout like grass and all evildoers flourish, “they will be forever destroyed.” (Psalm 92:7) Grass that shoots up fast looks impressive for a while. But the song says how it ends.

Honored is a tempting one, since the wicked can look like they're winning. But the verse says, “they will be forever destroyed.” (Psalm 92:7) Sprouting like grass and flourishing is only the first half of that sentence. The ending is where the songwriter lands.

Remembered is a sneaky one, friend. The verse doesn't go there. It says that though the wicked sprout like grass and all evildoers flourish, “they will be forever destroyed.” (Psalm 92:7) Flourishing for a while is the setup. Destroyed is the word the songwriter chose.

True, and he says it short and strong: “But You, O LORD, are exalted forever!” (Psalm 92:8) After all that talk about the wicked, he turns and points straight at the LORD. One line, no wasted words. I could learn something from that.

Not false, friend. Right after the warning about the wicked, the songwriter says, “But You, O LORD, are exalted forever!” (Psalm 92:8) It's a tiny line, easy to blow past. It carries a lot for its size.
That's it, friend. The songwriter says, “My eyes see the downfall of my enemies…” (Psalm 92:11) That's what his eyes see. He doesn't say how or when it happened, only what he sees.

explanations.answer: The LORD's glory in the temple
explanations.explanation: Glory in the temple sounds lovely, but it's not what this verse says. The songwriter says, “My eyes see the downfall of my enemies…” (Psalm 92:11) That's the thing his eyes see. The temple isn't mentioned in this line.

explanations.answer: A great harvest in the land
explanations.explanation: A great harvest would be a nice thing to see, friend. Not in this verse, though. The songwriter says, “My eyes see the downfall of my enemies…” (Psalm 92:11) That's what his eyes see. A harvest would have been a happier line, I'll admit.

A palm tree, friend. The songwriter says, “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree, and grow like a cedar in Lebanon.” (Psalm 92:12) The wicked were grass. The righteous get a tree. That's quite the upgrade.

A wildflower is a pretty picture, but the songwriter picked something taller. He says, “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree…” (Psalm 92:12) Earlier the wicked were compared to grass. Now we're up in the trees.

A reed by the river is a nice image, friend, but it's not this one. The verse says, “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree, and grow like a cedar in Lebanon.” (Psalm 92:12) Both of those are trees. The songwriter went tall and sturdy.

Other way around, friend. The songwriter says, “In old age they will still bear fruit; healthy and green they will remain.” (Psalm 92:14) So old age doesn't stop the fruit. The verse says they keep bearing it. That's good news for anybody with soft edges, and I'm raising my hand.
False is right. The songwriter says, “In old age they will still bear fruit; healthy and green they will remain.” (Psalm 92:14) The word is still. Old age doesn't shut the bakery down.

explanations.answer: To proclaim what the LORD is like
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The verse says they remain that way “to proclaim, ‘The LORD is upright; He is my Rock, and in Him there is no unrighteousness.’” (Psalm 92:15) So the song ends with the proclaiming, which is where it started. It opened with praise and it closes with praise.

explanations.answer: To shade the courts of the temple
explanations.explanation: Shade is a clever guess, since we've been talking trees. But the verse doesn't say that. The righteous remain healthy and green “to proclaim, ‘The LORD is upright…’” (Psalm 92:15) The point is the proclaiming. Nobody's handing out shade.

explanations.answer: To feed the poor of the land
explanations.explanation: Feeding the poor is a good thing, and the Bible talks about it elsewhere. Not in this verse, though, friend. Here they stay healthy and green “to proclaim, ‘The LORD is upright; He is my Rock…’” (Psalm 92:15) What they proclaim is the point.
